sources.note: tiles n19w156, n20w155, n20w156, n20w157, n21w156, n21w157, n21w158, n22w157, n22w158, n22w159, n22w160, n22w161, n23w160, n23w161; the other 66 one-degree cells in the box have no tile (no land; Nihoa, at 23.06° N 161.92° W, lies in n24w162, which the USGS does not publish, so it is sea here); a texel is land where at least half its area is land in the DEM, and then takes the area-weighted mean of the land cells (never below 0.25 m)

subsidence.rule: a volcano sinks at r0 while its shield builds and at r0·exp(−τ/τ0) after, τ the time since its shield ended, fitted (least squares on ln r) to the measured rates below; where a volcano rises (Oʻahu on the arch) it stood lower by that uplift; at a stage a volcano stands higher than today by what it has sunk since, a field that blends the volcanoes by distance and tapers to nothing at the base
subsidence.ruleNotUsed: volcanoes.json's subsidenceRule (2.6 mm a year for 1 Ma after a shield, then 0.01) lifts every young shield 2600 m, which in this model joins Oʻahu to Penguin Bank and Molokaʻi from 2 Ma and Maui Nui to Oʻahu at 1.2 Ma; the curve fitted to the measured rates is used instead (bake-geology.mjs --subsidence rule draws the rule)

profile.rule: z(d) at distance d from a summit of height h: above sea level h − d·tan(α); below it, the slope of each 500 m band of depth; down to the base. Fitted to the median heights by distance on the sectors named, from the seafloor pack.

fittedTo.why: the south-west rift and the Kona flank, away from Hualālai, Mauna Kea and Kīlauea
the south flank, from the summit to the toe of the Hilina bench

hotspot.positionNote: Between Kīlauea and Kamaʻehuakanaloa, the volcanoes over it now (Clague and Sherrod 2014, p. 97); the point is the midpoint of their summits.
hotspot.speedNote: The line of volcano birth in Clague and Sherrod’s fig. 14 (p. 122) has a slope of 10 cm/yr, “average plate motion”. Moore and Clague (1992) find the end of shield building moving south-east at about 13 cm/yr from Haleakalā to Hualālai.

speedAlternatives.note: end-of-shield progression, Haleakalā to Hualālai, toward S 40° E

hotspot.azimuthUnit: degrees, compass, the direction the plate carries a volcano
hotspot.azimuthNote: Derived here, not read: the mean bearing from Kīlauea’s summit to the summits of Kauaʻi, Niʻihau, Waiʻanae and Koʻolau in Clague and Sherrod’s table 1 (kauai 303.6°, niihau 299.1°, waianae 307.8°, koolau 309.4°). A stage at age A is drawn displaced by A × speed toward the opposite bearing.

displacement.formula: a stage at age A (Ma) is drawn moved by A × speed toward the bearing azimuth + 180° (the islands slide back along the plate's path as the age runs down): x_m += 1e4 · A · speed · sin(azimuth + 180°), z_m −= 1e4 · A · speed · cos(azimuth + 180°), speed in cm a year, x east and z south in metres in the shared projection (DATA.md §1); the whole stage image moves as one, since the plate carries every volcano on it together

stages.label: Kauaʻi and Niʻihau, complete and alone
stages.rule: sea level as today (0 m); land ≥ 0.25 m, sea ≤ −1 m. Complete shields, or within 15% of their full height (Niʻihau, summit 1493 m, lifted 1150 m, 95% of its erosion still to come; Kauaʻi, 95% grown (its shield ends at 4 Ma), summit 2564 m, today's shape raised 1036 m): below -2600 m today the sea floor as it is now, lifted by the subsidence since; above -2000 m the profile at the summit, blended toward today's lifted surface as its erosion runs, by (A / shield end)² of the difference still to go. Shields still building (none): the profile alone. Not yet begun (Waiʻanae, Koʻolau, Penguin Bank, West Molokaʻi, East Molokaʻi, West Maui, Lānaʻi, Kahoʻolawe, Haleakalā, Kohala, Mauna Kea, Hualālai, Mauna Loa, Kīlauea, Kamaʻehuakanaloa, Kaʻula, Māhukona): the base.
